title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
Udio, an AI music generation service launched in 2024, trained its models on recorded music without obtaining licenses from the rights holders. Major labels alleged that this training process reproduced copyrighted material without authorization, which is the central failure mode here: a system built using data that the builder did not have permission to use. The problem was not in how the tool performed at the point of user interaction but in what was ingested during the training phase, before any song was ever generated for a consumer.

Universal Music Group settled its lawsuit against Udio and Warner Music Group did the same, with both deals pointing toward future platforms trained only on licensed material. Sony Music filed a separate new lawsuit asserting infringement across more than 30,000 recordings, a judge declined to let Sony add those recordings to its original case, and Sony then filed a second standalone suit. A class action brought by independent artists was also allowed to proceed, though the venue was moved. A musicians' union separately sued UMG over the settlement terms themselves.

What is not established is that any court has found Udio liable for copyright infringement; the lawsuits and the Sony allegations are claims, not verdicts, and the settlements do not constitute admissions of wrongdoing under the facts reported here.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit accusing Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The music creation platform allows users to generate original songs with AI from text prompts. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, where artists can opt in to have their work included and receive compensation. UMG, which owns rights to songs like The Temptations' "My Girl," did not disclose the financial terms of the settlement.

This marks Udio's first major licensing deal with a major music label. The New York-based startup, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am and Andreessen Horowitz, has attracted millions of users since its release. The settlement demonstrates a shift toward cooperation between the music industry and AI companies after months of legal disputes over copyright infringement. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
